utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Welcome to everyone I think for the first time in this courtroom during this trial. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand, Mr. Harmon, that you'd like to address the Chamber before we continue the examination-in-chief of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I would, Your Honour. Thank you very much. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, Counsel. Monday morning, Mr. Stewart proposed in part a schedule that would start the testimony of Mr. Treanor following the conclusion of the direct examination of Mr. Deronjic, and that was of course the first time I had heard that proposal. My response to that proposal, as Your Honours are aware, was that it was not possible because we were in the process of organising and preparing Mr. Treanor's exhibits. Now, that position was an apparent contradiction to information that the Trial Chamber had received earlier as to the availability of Mr. Treanor. At the end of Monday's session, Judge Orie, speaking on behalf of the Trial Chamber, expressed surprise and said, and I quote: "And let me be quite clear that one day being ready and the other day not being ready any more needs at least some explanation the Chamber has not received yet." And Judge Orie continued: "In general terms, this change of position by the Prosecution perhaps should have been announced prior to telling this Chamber in Court." Now, I accept that, and with your permission, I would like to provide that explanation to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I can imagine that it has got something to do with the difficulties we faced when looking at exhibits on our screen, so that the Prosecution had to change its approach to how to present documents. If that -- because I've been thinking about what could have caused it, what came into my mind. If that would be it, a short explanation would do, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, that indeed is it precisely. On Monday morning, we were prepared to proceed with Mr. Treanor's testimony and all of his exhibits were in electronic format. However, events the previous week, particularly in respect of the intercepts, caused me considerable concern in trying to fashion a remedy that would best assist the Trial Chamber in having the exhibits at hand and being able to analyse those exhibits properly. So on Friday afternoon, late Friday afternoon, I instructed my staff to prepare all exhibits that related to the intercepts that we were going to be presenting in Court in a different fashion. The fashion that Your Honour saw had the script moving too fast, you were unable to see the full intercept itself, the text, and therefore judge and assess the context and what was being said. So as I say, I instructed my staff to prepare hard copies of all intercepts that were going to be presented in Court. The calculation that we had on Friday when I gave that instruction was that Mr. Treanor was not going to be testifying until at the end of this week, Friday or perhaps early the following week, so when I gave that instruction on Friday late afternoon, that instruction I knew when I heard the proposal of Mr. Stewart was not going to be implemented. It was not in the process of being implemented on Monday morning when I heard that proposal. And therefore, Your Honours, I made my response to Your Honour, saying we were in the process of preparing and organising our exhibits. So that change in circumstance is precisely why I made that comment to Your Honours and why I said I would not be ready. Following Monday presentation of evidence, and we went through a series of problems with the documents themselves and being visible on the computer monitors, and having to go through each exhibit paragraph by paragraph on the ELMO. Once again, I came to the conclusion that we weren't assisting the Trial Chamber in the best way we could in taking our evidence and looking at our evidence and being able to analyse the evidence. So on Monday, after Court, I instructed again my colleagues to prepare all of Mr. Treanor's be exhibits in hard copy for each of Your Honours and counsel so that they would be available. So that, Your Honours, is the explanation that I offer to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That explanation leads to better understanding, Mr. Harmon. Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have just three additional small points.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If respect of Prosecutor's Exhibit 60, which is this map, a small -- an enlarged map of Glogova, taken from a map of one -- of a scale of 1:100.000, Your Honours asked me to inform you of what the scale is of this enlarged version of it, and I can tell you now the scale is one centimetre to 71.428 centimetres. The next issue I can inform Your Honours about is Prosecutor's Exhibit 37, an exhibit that had superfluous text at the bottom of the exhibit. Your Honours asked me to provide a copy to the registrar without that text and just to inform Your Honours, we have done so. And the last item deals with the witness Mr. Rasid Hasanovic, whose status we continue to monitor. The essence of it is this: Mr. Hasanovic still needs proper travel papers to leave the United States to get here. He has not received those papers. We will continue to monitor the situation, and my suggestion, and I've discussed this with counsel, but my suggestion would be this: If he does not have his travel papers by the end of the weekend, given that Mr. Treanor's testimony will carry over into next week in all likelihood, my suggestion would be that we abandon for this session calling Mr. Hasanovic, because -- and unless he could complete his testimony in one sitting, because otherwise it would require Mr. Hasanovic coming from the United States to testify in part and then have to return during the next session from the United States. I think that would be an expense that could be avoided and should be avoided, and I -- with the Court's permission, I would be prepared to inform the Court on Monday what the final situation is as of that date, as to the status of Mr. Hasanovic. We can better judge where the examination of Mr. Treanor is at that point and make a better judgement then as to whether Mr. Hasanovic should be brought to Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there any explanation as to why papers for travelling are not -- I mean, usually you get papers from governments. Is there any --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I can tell Your Honour what I understand the situation to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It's all as a result of post 9/11 fallout in the United States. With the Homeland Security Department, Mr. Hasanovic needs special papers because he doesn't have a US passport. He needs special papers to be able to leave the United States, given his status in the United States and he needs those papers so he can return to the United States. So it's very complicated. I find it myself, like you, this should be something that should be easily resolved. Unfortunately, it has not been and we have pressed the issue and we continue to do so, but that's what I can offer Your Honours as an explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that, especially since it's your witness, that you emphasise, wherever you can, that it's necessary for him to come. Whenever you would need the assistance of the Chamber in that respect, we will hear from you, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any observation to be made on the part of the Defence, 71.428 perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, not on that or anything else at this moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stewart. Then, Mr. Harmon, is the Prosecution ready to continue the examination-in-chief of Mr. Deronjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We are, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then may I ask the security and the usher to escort Mr. Deronjic into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Deronjic. Good afternoon. Please be seated. I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony, and I take it that you still remember my words spoken at that occasion. Mr. Harmon, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Deronjic.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, we concluded your testimony on Monday. You had described attending a meeting in Pale, where you had informed various people that the population from the village of Glogova had been transferred, a large part of the village had been burned, and the operations in the Bratunac municipality and the surrounding settlements were continuing. Now, Mr. Deronjic, were you, after you gave that report, or during the time you gave that report, were you criticised by Mr. Karadzic for the actions that you described having taken?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He did not criticise me for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were you criticised by Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't criticise me either.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were you criticised by Mr. Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, other than Mr. Djeric, about whom we're going to be talking in a minute, were you ever criticised by anyone from the SDS Main Board or from the Bosnian Serb government about the actions that you had taken in respect of Glogova and other Muslim settlements in the Bratunac municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but if I may add something briefly, with your permission.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not until 1993 did I have opportunity to meet with these people, due to the war-related events in Bratunac. In the summer of 1992, I went to Pale again, but I don't remember going to the government during that period. So there was no possibility for anyone to criticise me directly, except from the fact that I told about these events to a representative of the government who came to Bratunac to inform the War Presidency or the government commission, or whatever it was called, of what was going on, and it was to him that I related the events that had taken place in Glogova. He made some notes, but he did not criticise me in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you identify that person?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Mr. Djokanovic, who was a deputy to the Joint Assembly. He was the president of a rather small party during the pre-war era, which was called the Federalist Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What was his first name, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot at this point, but I will probably remember, because I know the man.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, after you left this particular meeting that you described to us, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After this meeting, I went to the government to see Mr. Djeric, the president of the government of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And clarify in my own mind: Was he the president or was he the prime minister of the government of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the prime minister, or, as he's commonly referred to in our language, the president of the government of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Why did you go see him?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to inform Mr. Djeric as well of what had happened, because during the previous meeting, the meeting that I had attended, was focussed more on briefing. I didn't hear any serious comment on anything, and I wanted to inform the prime minister of the events in Bratunac. So I went to see him and I told him more or less the same version of the events that I had described previously at the meeting, because I wanted to hear what he thought of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What specifically did you tell Mr. Djeric?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I told him that we had undertaken an action in which the military had also taken part, the Yugoslav People's Army, that is, the Territorial Defence and the police, and that in the course of that action, we forcibly removed the population of Glogova to the territory under the Muslim control, specifically, to Kladanj. And I also told him that the epilogue and the consequence of this event was the burning of the village, which had almost completely been set on fire. At that point, I wasn't aware of any killing, so I wasn't able to tell him anything about that, but as for the rest of the events, I described them the way they had occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What was Mr. Djeric's reaction to that account?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will just summarise his reaction, because I don't remember the entire conversation. He was very angry. He was upset and angrily he asked me: Who ordered this? Why was this done in this way? And I explained to him that this had been done pursuant to my orders and that I had also informed the meeting which preceded this encounter, of this. Djeric made some notes of what I had told him, but, in brief, he was very angry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, how do you account for the different reactions between Mr. Djeric, who was angry, and Mr. Mladic, Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Ostojic and the other representatives, those representatives applauded you for what you reported. How do you account for that difference?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do have an explanation of sorts. I can give it to you. I will try to be as brief as possible. In my testimonies so far, I have maintained that, as far as the plans of this kind were concerned, the plans which implied the participation of the volunteers, the transfer of the population from certain areas, the forcible removal of the population, and so on and so forth, that the entire leadership of Republika Srpska was not aware of all of these plans. And I'm referring to two or three individuals with whom I talked later on. I met with Mr. Djeric in the summer of 1992, in Zvornik, at a meeting which was attended by regional officials of the SDS and representatives of municipal authorities. And I could see that Mr. Djeric was not informed of the details of the early days of the war in the Eastern Herzegovina. He inquired about what had happened. He made notes of what he heard, and he expressed his disagreement with the events that had taken place. And I also had an opportunity, two or three times, maybe, to discuss the issue with President Koljevic, sometime in 1993, I believe, in Milici. Koljevic used to be my professor from the university. And I knew him personally. He too was surprised at the course of the events in Eastern Bosnia. Later, I went to see him at Pale, and we discussed this once again, and he again told me that he had not been aware of this type of activities that had taken place in Eastern Bosnia. I told him my opinion, that is, this had taken place according to a plan, that someone must have been behind the arrival of these volunteers. And again, I believe we discussed the issue once when we met in Zvornik, at home -- at the home of a small entrepreneur there. He invited me specifically to discuss these events, and once again, he told me that he had not been aware of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So let me ask you, Mr. Deronjic: After the conclusion of this meeting with Mr. Djeric, did you return to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember at this point where I went.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were you informed as to the situation in respect of the Muslim detainees in the Vuk Karadzic school?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you talking about the time when I returned from the meeting that was held on the 11th, at Pale?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I misunderstood your question. I thought you were referring to what happened after the meeting with Djeric in Zvornik. After the meeting at Pale, I went back to Bratunac and I was informed on the next day, because I had arrived rather late that night, so the next day I was informed that the people who had been separated at the stadium were detained in a facility, an abandoned facility which was some kind of workshop, commonly referred to as the hangar. I have also seen this word being used in various documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What did you do once you received that information?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Following these events, we held several sessions, in parallel with the events, actually. On the first or the second day, we tried to reinforce the control because we had received information that people were being taken out of this hangar, and we had information that some of them had been killed on the very first day. In addition to that, apparently some people had been severely beaten up inside the hangar itself. We then talked to the military police. I had a meeting with the commander of the military police, and we requested that the situation be dealt with as soon as possible and that entry be prohibited to outsiders. We didn't see --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the name.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- on that day, although we looked for him and we received a decision on his expulsion on account of several things, several criminal activities that he had been engaged during that period. We then asked our police to reinforce their presence there during the first couple of days, because we didn't know what to do with these people. When we realised that Reljic was mostly absent from Bratunac during these days, that we had to take care of these people, and when we realised that the killings were continuing, at a session held right after these events, we adopted a decision to release these people. We made a list of them, and then secretly, at about 2.00 a.m., we let them go. We took them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me stop you there for just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, the interpreter said on page 12, line 6 that the name was not heard. Mr. Deronjic, you said that you -- after the meeting with the commander, you requested that the situation be dealt with as soon as possible and that entry be prohibited to outsiders. You then said: "We didn't see," and you mentioned a name, "...that day," although you looked for him. Could you please repeat the name of who you didn't see and you were looking for.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mentioned two men. This is for the interpreter, so that it's clear. I spoke to the commander of the military police. His name was Savo Babic. The commander of the military unit, Mr. Reljic, he was the one that I couldn't find that day in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, what information did you receive about who was killing these detainees?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I got the information from the military police and the civilian police that volunteers were going inside and that -- and also some people from Srebrenica. And I'm primarily thinking of Mr. Drago Zekic, the father of the late Goran Zekic, who used to take people out, and he took them somewhere. I was told that he was doing this in order to monitor the investigation regarding the killing of his son. However, a large number of people never returned, so it was assumed that they were killed. I also have to say that I was told that there were some local people who had joined the volunteers, and they also went into the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you receive any information as to how many of the detainees had been killed?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My information in that period - and I'm talking about those days - I had information that a large number or many people were taken out, but nobody knew exactly how many were taken out over that period and killed. I was told, I think sometime on the 13th, that a group was taken to the Drina and that they were killed. I personally went there to see that, and I really did see several corpses in the water. I can't remember how many people were killed there, but I saw three or four corpses in the Drina River. And later, when these people were buried, when all the steps were completed in that sense, I got a different figure for the number of killed. I think the municipality must have a list of how many people were identified and buried there. I received different information, so I'm afraid to make a mistake, but I did have information at one point that a hundred people were killed. Later, I had information that the figures ranged from 50 to 60 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, the people who were detained in the hangar were Muslim civilians who had been removed from the Muslim settlements; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that you had prepared a list.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And if I could have the next exhibit number and have that exhibit shown to Mr. Deronjic and a copy of this exhibit handed to the Judges.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit number P61.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, if you would take a moment just to inspect Prosecutor's Exhibit 61 that is before you.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you recognise that exhibit, Mr. Deronjic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon. This is a list of people that we took to Pale from the hangar that night and handed over to a certain Marinkovic in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Just to orient everybody as to this exhibit: On the right-hand column of that exhibit, under residents, it indicates where these people were from; is that correct? And one can see --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: One can see many entries from Suha and other locations in Bratunac. Now, Mr. Deronjic, after you prepared this list, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the evening, after the decision that we adopted, at 2.00 a.m., we took those people, with a military and civilian police escort, and there were people who were entrusted as commanders to take care of those people. We transported them to Pale, where these commanders were supposed to hand them over to somebody from the civilian or military leadership of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, earlier you mention that had Pale was the capital of the Republika Srpska, and was that the location where Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik had their offices?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In respect of the Muslim civilians from Glogova in your testimony, you described they were put on various forms of transportation and moved to Kladanj, which was Bosnian-Muslim-held territory. My question, Mr. Deronjic, is: Why weren't these 400 detainees put on a bus and sent to Kladanj? Why were they sent to Pale?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will answer that question. I had strong personal reasons for doing that. In the beginning, when the volunteers came to Bratunac, I took a series of steps and measures to prevent their activities or to reduce them to a reasonable degree. However, due to a series of circumstances, we did not manage to do that entirely. I believed, even though I ordered the action on Glogova, and even though I participated in it in the way that I described, I agreed to certain things, which I did, but I never agreed to that, nor did I ever order or wish that people are killed. In that period or during the war, I never agreed to anything like that. Of course, I'm talking about people being killed for no reason, civilians. I'm not talking about people who are participating in combat. Due to a series of events in Bratunac, and due to the fact that this policy brought some disastrous results for Bratunac, I was angry and I decided to send these people directly to Pale. I wanted to say: Here you are. This is the result of what you have been doing. Here are these people, and you decide what you want to do with these people. This is a decision that I cannot make. So I left it up to them to deal with the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What was the reaction, as far as you know, as to the arrival of these 400 people who had been cleansed from the Bratunac municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reaction was quite strong. They didn't want to accept them at first. Everybody felt that the responsibility for that should be borne by somebody else, so they didn't know what to do with those people. The negotiations lasted for two or three days. I spoke to the commanders and I said that they were not to return those people to Bratunac under any circumstances, and if there was no other solution, they should just release them and let them come back to their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And when you say, "Negotiations," negotiations with whom?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commanders were negotiating. The police and the -- the military and civilian police commanders were negotiators. Mr. Josipovic from the civilian police and Babic from the military police were in charge of those people, so they were talking about the problem with some people who were there from the police and the military. I don't know those people. I didn't meet them later. I didn't meet Marinkovic either, the person who signed the document once he accepted to take over those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was there any reaction on the part of the Bosnian Serb leadership to the arrival of 400 Bosnian Muslim detainees who had been cleansed from Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that point, I don't know whether anybody from the leadership intervened in this matter. Once, during the war, I did have occasion to be reprimanded, in a way, by one of those people from the leadership, who said: "Why did you send those people over?" But I didn't really respond to that. I don't know exactly what I said, but this was my explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Who was it who reprimanded you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that -- well, I don't think. It was Karadzic, actually, during a conversation, just a regular conversation. He mentioned it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What happened to those 400 Muslim detainees?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, based on information I received -- again, I say I think because it's a little difficult for me to remember everything in detail. I think that those people were exchanged for some people in the Ilijas municipality -- or, excuse me, for some Serbs from the Ilijas municipality. But I don't know exactly when this happened and how.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In other words, they didn't return to the Bratunac municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Is that correct: They did not return to the Bratunac municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, at some point in time, Mr. Deronjic, in respect of the people who had been killed in the hangars, does a Dr. Stankovic appear in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, if you're thinking of Mr. Stankovic, the military pathologist from Belgrade. He came to Bratunac, at the invitation of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And very briefly, can you tell the Judges what he did.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the people were transported to Pale, we took a series of actions. First of all, we decided to expel all the volunteers from the Bratunac municipality. Then we called somebody from the military, from the Yugoslav People's Army to come and to examine the people who were killed, the bodies. Mr. Stankovic came, Zoran Stankovic. I think that was his name. Today he's the chief of the military medical academy in Belgrade, and he's a well-known pathologist. Accompanied by one officer whose name I don't know. I didn't remember it. They examined all the bodies, identified them, and then we talked to him about how we would bury those people. They were placed in nylon body bags. They were marked by numbers. Each body was identified and they were buried next to one another at a location which was set aside for that. They were buried publicly. We even ordered Muslim gravestones, but we never actually placed the gravestones on the graves because we were afraid of the reaction of the people. So that those gravestones are still in Bratunac today. After that, we adopted a decision to expel Mr. Reljic, and once he found out about the decision, he fled; he just took a car and he took some items, some things from Bratunac, and left.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did those bodies that had been buried remain in that location?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The bodies are not there any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What happened to those bodies?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The bodies were removed. I don't know who did it or when this was done. I know that a man came in 1994 who was interested in those bodies. I explained to him the situation, that they were buried publicly, that we identified them, buried them, and recorded their burial places, and that there was no need to touch them. Later, those people, as far as I know, those bodies, are no longer there. But I really don't know when and who did that. I can maybe just tell you what my assumptions are about who removed the bodies and when this was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, Mr. Deronjic: Who was it -- who was the man who came with whom you had a conversation about bodies?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was General Subotic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did he tell you why he was in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He said that he was interested in the graves in Bratunac, that he had a report that there were graves in Bratunac, and he asked me whether this was true and what I knew about it. I told him that the only grave that I knew of was this grave, that it's not a secret grave. I explained everything to him. I took him to the location. I showed it to him. It's near the road, near the settlement, close to that road. I told him: This is where we buried them. And I explained to him how we did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Deronjic. I have just a few more questions, and I would like to clean up parts of this transcript. And with your assistance, Mr. Deronjic, and unfortunately, Your Honours, I don't have the official transcript. I have the LiveNote, and I can cite to the LiveNote reference or later give Your Honours the transcript cites on the corrected version, but I can quote the answer and ask Mr. Deronjic to clarify a point so the record is clear. Mr. Deronjic, on the 16th of February, you provided the following answer. This is found, Your Honours, on the LiveNote at page 42 for that day. What I would like to correct is found on line 24. Let me read you the answer, Mr. Deronjic, and then I will ask you a question. You answered, in response to a question that I put to you, my question being: "Now, after the first group of volunteers was killed by the forces of Naser Oric, what happened?" Your answer was: "Two things happened, two things which would be of some significance for the future development of the events. A JNA unit arrived in the area. I had never seen this unit before, nor did I have any knowledge in that period as to the identity of that unit, but it was an armoured unit, consisting of perhaps 20 troops, and five to six armoured vehicles. Captain Suljic --" and my record shows S-u-l-j-i-c -- "...was their leader." Is that the correct name for the leader of that particular group?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know how this mistake occurred, but the correct name of the commander of that group is Captain Reljic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me turn to another portion of this transcript in order to correct it. This is found on page 89 of the LiveNote. The correction I am going to be directing the witness's attention to is found at line 10. And the answer, Mr. Deronjic, I will read part of the answer, starting at line 5: "I said that the day before, the 9th of May, we carried out the forcible transfer of the population of Glogova, that the village was torched, most of the village was torched and that all the inhabitants of the village who happened to be there when we came were evacuated in the direction of Kladovo." Is that the direction that they went?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's a mistake. We're talking about Kladanj. That is the name of the municipality, which is the neighbouring municipality to Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Finally, Mr. Deronjic, I'd like to direct your attention to answers that you gave in respect of the meeting that took place with Mr. Zekic in the Hotel Fontana on the 5th of May, and referring to page 60, I'm going to read part of your answer, starting at line 12 and ending at line 16: "I wanted to know under whose orders they were acting, and he said one sentence which I remembered to this date, that this was all pursuant to an agreement and that the arrival of the military in Bratunac had been based on an agreement between the leadership of Serbia and the leadership of Republika Srpska." Now, Mr. Deronjic, that was your answer. Later in your testimony, at page 66, page 66, lines 19 through 24, you were asked a question by Judge Orie. And his question was: "Is it on the basis of his words that you knew what he was referring to or that you presumed what he was referring to, or was it on the basis of knowledge outside, obtained outside of that conversation?" Your answer, as interpreted, was as follows: "He said -- I cannot quote his exact words, but he said that there had been an agreement between the highest organs of Republika Srpska and those in Serbia with respect to the operations that were conducted in the area. So on the basis of that, I was able to assume that he was referring to the highest organs. Obviously, he was not referring to low-level organs. I was a low-level organ myself." So, Mr. Deronjic, I'd like to focus on the term "organ," because it may cause some confusion. What did you mean by the term "organ" in the answer I just read you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I mentioned the term "organ" several times. I'm thinking of the top leadership. I'm thinking of a state organ, either the Presidency or the government or a military organ. And when I said that -- when I mentioned a local level organ, I was thinking of the Crisis Staff. At the time, it was the organ of authority at the local level.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That concludes my direct examination, Your Honour. Mr. Deronjic, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, this concludes your examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It does, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I please ask you one question about Exhibit P61, just presented to the witness. You have provided the Chamber, and I take it also the Defence, not only with P61, but also with P61.1. I expect at least that it gets that number. That's the English translation. Because I have some problems with it. If I look at your list of exhibits, the last exhibit is this list of 401 Muslims. You give as the document date, you give the 17th of May, 1992, and it seems that you refer to it as document OTP reference 34031A, whereas the translation seems to bear the same number, but now with "B" instead of "A." In the translation, we find, on the -- not on the front page but on the first page to follow, not being just a form, where it says at the bottom: "Pale, 14th of May, 1992." At the same time, you indicate the 17th of May as the document date on the list, and I can imagine that the confusion comes from the original, which gives a figure that might be read perhaps both as a 7 or as a 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I can see the confusion, Your Honour. I can see where one could take this figure on the original could be interpreted as a 4 or a 7. But that's the source of the confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's -- but you solved the problem at one in a 7 and at another moment the interpreters, at least, solved it as being a 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm not sure what I can do in respect of interpreting this particular person's penmanship. It's quite confusing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps I could ask your attention for the following: There where the date appears, the date which seems not to be very clear, we find handwriting, and I especially draw your attention to the word "Pale," as such a word, that we also find on the front page of that same document, which, although I'm not an expert, seems to have a striking resemblance, the handwriting seems to have a striking resemblance with -- on the front page, in this first page. And to my surprise, I find a figure 4 on the cover page, which differs quite a bit from the number we were just discussing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I certainly agree with Your Honour. What I don't see in the 7 on the third page is a strike mark across the vertical part of the figure itself, which I think is customary in Europe. I can't resolve this, Your Honour. I don't have a way to resolve this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is just to make clear that this could create some confusion, and how important it is, we'll find out at a later stage. If you could solve the matter in one way or the other, or if the witness could, we'll hear from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I can put this exhibit to the witness, Your Honour, and ask him if he can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: -- make that distinction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, you have given him quite some clues, and it would be -- I would like to know what the basis would be for his interpretation. If he knows exactly about the dates, fine, but I'm not waiting for his interpretation of this same information we just discussed. So if he has any knowledge, fine, but I'd rather not have his expertise on the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, do you have Prosecutor's Exhibit 61 in front of you? Mr. Deronjic, let me direct your attention to the third page, where there's a signature at the bottom. It says, the last line, it says, "Pale," and there's a date. Do you know when this particular document was created? If you do, please tell us; if you don't, don't answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say when it was created, with great certainty; however, not a hundred per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: May I invite the witness to answer that question, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but not only to give the answer to the question, but also on the basis of what he comes to this conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If you can provide us with the answer, Mr. Deronjic, and then please tell us the basis for your answer.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We adopted the decision to release these people in the night between the 13th and the 14th. I don't think that there's any possibility for these people to have arrived and to have been handed over on the 14th, because there was talk about them being held up there for a day or two. So I believe that the document was created on the 17th.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Deronjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, again, I've concluded my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Harmon. Mr. Stewart, is the Defence ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I invite you to start cross-examining the witness, and keep in mind that we would like to have a break at approximately a quarter to 4.00. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, earlier on in your evidence in this case, you - excuse me one moment - you said that you had had an opportunity to meet and discuss with SDS leaders, both on a local, municipal level, on a regional level, and on the republican level, policies of both the SDS party and the government, and you said that you had had that opportunity from the time you joined the SDS party and assumed your first responsibilities. Whether you specifically recall saying that, that -- you're content with that as evidence from you, are you? You're nodding. It's probably better if you say something into the microphone so that the tape can pick it up.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I'm waiting for the interpreters to finish interpreting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because they still go on after you have finished. So can I please ask you to tell me your name so I can address you properly. I didn't get your name.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Of course. My name is Nicholas Stewart, and I think the normal form of address would simply be Mr. Stewart, if you feel comfortable with that. I do if you do.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you so much. Mr. Stewart, I do remember saying this, and I maintain what I said, that is, that I had opportunity throughout those years to meet with these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But isn't it correct that certainly, at least in the early years, for perhaps four or five years, from 1990 onwards, you never had any opportunity to discuss with Mr. Krajisnik personally any such matters?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, what you say, that I never had any opportunity to contact Mr. Krajisnik personally at that period, is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And in fact, you -- where you said, just to clarify, in your evidence, you were asked whether you -- whether you knew the accused, Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik, and you said of course that you also know him. But it's -- you knew him, of course, in the sense that from 1990, you knew who he was.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. In 1990, I don't remember any encounter with him, be it at meetings or personal encounters. However, in 1991, I did see him at some of the meetings, but, to be precise, I did not have any personal contact with Mr. Krajisnik at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Are you quite sure you're talking about 1991 in your last answer?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw Mr. Krajisnik in 1991, at the meetings that I spoke about, namely, in April, and in the autumn of 1995, but I did not have personal contact with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. So in 1991, you simply saw Mr. Krajisnik, did you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But never had any personal discussion with him at all?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No in the sense of correct, you're agreeing with what I've just put to you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer is: No, I did not have any personal contact with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You see the slight ambiguity sometimes there is in the word "no" as an answer. It's happened before, so I may sometimes follow that up. The -- because you did say in your evidence earlier that except through the media, you personally didn't know Mr. Krajisnik in 1991. So you're adding to knowledge through the media that you at least saw him at some meeting or other during that year?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I merely saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And what meeting or meetings are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about two meetings. In April 1991 and in December 1991, when a session of Republika Srpska was held, that is, when the Assembly of Republika Srpska was established. I'm talking about the session held on the 15th of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, if we're talking, then, about those -- you're talking about those particular meetings in April 1991 and December 1991 that you've already given answers about at some length in your evidence in this case. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, we'll come back to those meetings specifically. So to make it clear, then: Subject to your seeing Mr. Krajisnik possibly at those meetings, which we'll come to, your only occasion of seeing Mr. Krajisnik otherwise would have been on television; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right, but I allow for the possibility of the two of us having attended a larger meeting of some sort, but at this point I cannot remember any such meeting except for the two that I've mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. But without being trivial or flippant about it,

utterances.speaker: MR. DERONJIC
utterances.text: If you attended a larger meeting, you would have had the same contact with Mr. Krajisnik as if you had both gone to a football match separately.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, something to that effect. The Main Board has about a hundred people. If all of the officials are there, and usually they would attend local meetings of that kind in such large numbers. So yes, you would have a very large number of people attending those meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You said specifically in your evidence that in the course of 1992, you don't think you saw Mr. Krajisnik, so you mean you didn't see him at all in that year; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, I had contacts with Mr. Karadzic in 1992, and I cannot remember any encounter with Mr. Krajisnik in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In fact, you didn't have very great contact with Mr. Karadzic in those early years of the 1990s, did you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1990, yes, I did, mostly concerning the elections, drawing up the election lists, and so on and so forth. In 1991, there may have been other meetings which were perhaps not so important, mostly concerning the election results. And in 1992, I remember only the meeting with Mr. Karadzic which took place in the summer of 1992. So at this point, I cannot remember any other meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Let's go back to Mr. Krajisnik, then. You said that in 1993, you saw Mr. Krajisnik at meetings of the Personnel Commission; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. In 1993, the party resumed its work. The Personnel Commission resumed its work, and I saw Mr. Karadzic at those meetings at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik. You said Mr. Karadzic a moment ago. Was that a slip of the tongue? We were talking about Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My apologies. It could have been a slip of the tongue. I was referring to Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In 1993, then, as you say, you saw Mr. Krajisnik at meetings of the Personnel Commission, is it right that you only ever saw him at meetings of that commission during that year?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I also saw him at the meetings of the Main Board. The Vance-Owen Plan was discussed in 1993, and I remember that I was with the Main Board when this was discussed, and Mr. Krajisnik was also present there. So I did see him at the meetings of the Main Board and the meetings of the Personnel Commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What's the month when you joined the Main Board?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never got this decision, but I believe that this was in early summer 1993, and I think that it was in the month of February, at the so-called Jahorina plenary, that the party renewed, resumed, its work.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: February 1993?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But in the summer of -- early summer of 1993, you say you became a member of the Main Board; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You were -- the way you described it, I think you were on loan to the Main Board. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There may have been a mistake in interpretation. I was co-opted to the Main Board. I was not elected through a regular procedure at an assembly session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I'm going -- the translation has come through as co-option. I'm going to accept that as the proper equivalent of "loan." You -- in effect, it was because Mr. Zekic had been killed and he had been a member of the Main Board and you took his place?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can you say when you first went to a meeting of the Main Board?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And how many meetings of the Main Board can you remember attending in 1993?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember the number of meetings. It's quite impossible for me to recall. I do recall some of them. I may have been present at the meetings that I have simply forgotten about in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Certainly last Thursday you did apparently remember, because you said that you attended two or three such meetings. Does that jog your memory, or is it perhaps that that was a little bit too bold of you to try and put a number on it on Thursday?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried, yes. You are right. I cannot be precise. I did not attend all of the meetings. I know that - for various reasons. One of them being the fact that it was rather complicated and unsafe to travel to Pale. But once again, I'm not able to give you a precise answer, and if this is what you're interested in, I'm sorry, I cannot help you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What I'm interested in, Mr. Deronjic, can I make it clear, so that it will help everybody, I'm interested in the truth. If you're able to give a precise answer truthfully, please do; if you're not, please say that you can't. The -- is it correct that whatever the precise number who attended, that all meetings of the Main Board that you attended were attended by something of the order of about a hundred people?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, but it is an approximation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But that was all I was inviting, Mr. Deronjic, at that point. The -- what about the meetings of the Personnel Commission? How many -- in 1993, you were a member of that commission, and so was Mr. Krajisnik. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What was the total membership of that commission?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only give you an approximate number. Ten to 12 people, maximum 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And can you say how many meetings of the Personnel Commission you attended in the course of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot give you a precise number.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you attend any meetings of the Personnel Commission in 1993?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, I cannot be precise, but I think I did in 1993. I attended a large number of meetings, until it completed its mandate, but I don't know how many of those meetings took place in 1993, 1994, or 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was 1993 to 1995 your overall period of membership of that commission, you personally?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just say that I don't remember when the Personnel Commission was dissolved. I was its member during that period, and I also know that personnel affairs were dealt with by the Presidency of the SDS of Republika Srpska after that, but I don't remember the date when it ceased to function as an organ of the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So as best you can remember over your entire period of membership with the Personnel Commission, are you able to say approximately how many meetings of that commission you attended?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately ten. Ten for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So approximately ten, but you're sureness is that that approximate number of meetings was attended by you personally?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Really, these events which took place ten years ago, after all, escape my memory. I really cannot remember the exact number of these meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you said in your evidence earlier that you think in a majority of the cases of that Personnel Commission, Mr. Krajisnik attended; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So sometimes he was there and sometimes he wasn't?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And it seems to follow from what you've been saying that sometimes you were there and sometimes you weren't.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is quite possible that I was absent from some of the meetings. I didn't even attend all of the meetings of the Main Board. This is why I said that it is possible that I did not attend some of those meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What -- it may seem to you, Mr. Deronjic, self-explanatory, but what was the function of the Personnel Commission?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Personnel Commission dealt with the proposals of -- for appointments to state and political organs. Municipal boards submitted their proposals to the Personnel Commission, and then the Personnel Commission would review the relevant documents to check whether all legal requirements have been met. And then the decision on the final -- that is, the final decision on the proposal would be adopted by the Main Board, and then their proposals were then forwarded to various relevant authorities, who would then proceed with those appointments. So, in a nutshell, this was the main task of this Personnel Commission

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Who chaired the commission? Well, assuming it had a chair, as I suppose it must have done. Who chaired the commission when you first became a member?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic chaired all of the meetings that I attended.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was a typical meeting to rubber stamp a large proportion of the proposed appointments and debate only a very small number?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. It was impossible for us to know all of those individuals, so we dealt mostly with the technical and legal aspects of the cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And did you personally make a contribution to debates where there was an issue about appointment?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. Even if I did, it would have been only for the people from my area. But there were no such appointments in that period. I may have participated in some of the discussions, but I don't remember anything in particular about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, would that be a convenient point for the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it certainly is. We'll adjourn until five minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May the witness be escorted into the courtroom by the competent authorities. Please be seated, Mr. Deronjic. Mr. Stewart, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, in 1992 -- I beg your pardon. In 1991 and 1992, Mr. -- and then 1993, Mr. Krajisnik had his position as Speaker of the Bosnia-Herzegovinian Assembly, and of course later of the Republika Srpska Assembly, and he had his membership of the Personnel Commission; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Those -- that's the sum total of his positions, as far as you recall, during that period; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the post of the member of the Main Board of the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That really went with his position as Speaker, didn't it? In practical terms, he was bound to be on the Main Board, as Speaker of the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think that it was automatic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, I don't think we need to get into that. I'll leave that, whether it was technical or practical consequence, we needn't worry. But so the -- his position as member of the Personnel Commission, his position as Speaker of the Assembly and his membership of the Main Board. That's it, that's the sum total of his positions that you were aware of in the party; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you've already said that you -- well, your -- and your own personal knowledge about the policies of the SDS was fairly limited at that time, wasn't it, in 1991, 1992? You weren't involved yourself in formation of main policy of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you've said that later on, and only later on, after you were appointed a vice-president in 1996, then you could provide certain views on Mr. Krajisnik's influence and importance in Serbian politics.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You expressed an opinion of Mr. Krajisnik as a man of the highest trustworthiness in Serbian politics in general in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Is it correct that you have -- you've never heard or read anywhere of Mr. Krajisnik expressing any racial or nationalistic hatred toward anyone, have you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I never heard or read anything about racial hatred or any other form of conduct which would be illegal.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Or reprehensible in any moral sense; that's correct as well, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had the opportunity only once to -- or twice, to speak directly, not tete-a-tete, but facing face to face with Mr. Krajisnik. If you wish, I could tell you what we discussed, but I don't think that it's of too much importance. But I did not hear Mr. Krajisnik express any view which I would say was morally reprehensible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you're not, for example, you're not aware of any suggestion that any orders ever came from Mr. Krajisnik for destruction of mosques or destruction or attacks on any religious or cultural buildings, are you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And your not aware of Mr. Krajisnik having ever had any position of command in relation to any army or army units, or police or police units?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know of any information of that nature, i.e., that Mr. Krajisnik had any position of command in relation to the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And did you form, throughout the period in which you knew of Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Krajisnik's position, did you form a view of Mr. Krajisnik as a principled and positive influence on Serbian politics in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I formed an opinion about Mr. Krajisnik later. I believe, first of all, that he had a major influence on Serbian politics at the time I was a member of those higher political bodies. I believe that Mr. Krajisnik was a personal friend of Mr. Karadzic. I cannot remember any remarks by Mr. Krajisnik about the war, other than about the peace plans that we discussed, where positions were taken with regard to the peace plans that were on the agenda. The rest of the plans related to the work of the Assembly, which Mr. Krajisnik talked about, and during the Personnel Commission sessions, it was about candidates proposed by certain municipal boards. I couldn't answer in the affirmative about hearing any kind of morally problematic views. This was not the topic of the discussion, or I never heard any such thing being expressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Is it right that your knowledge of the actual work of the Speaker of the Assembly, and that would apply to both Assemblies, the Bosnia-Herzegovina Assembly and later the Serbian -- Serb Assembly, your knowledge of the actual work of the Speaker was really no more than an informed, intelligent person who could read the newspapers and watch television and engage in general discussion about political matters?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Thank you for the intelligent person attribute.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In -- let's just go back, then, on the topic of an intelligent person's information about politics. Some basic points. We know, don't we, that in -- on the 9th of November, 1990, there were elections and the what are called the nationalist parties won the day, the SDA, the HDZ, and the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And after those elections, Mr. Izetbegovic became the president?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president of Bosnia and Herzegovina, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Thank you for adding that for clarification. Mr. Izetbegovic became the president of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Mr. Krajisnik became the Speaker of the parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina, or the Assembly, the parliament; and a Croat, Mr. Jure Pelivan became the prime minister of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, all that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: How would you, Mr. Deronjic, summarise the main SDS policies at that time, after the election and when that power-sharing structure of government was adopted?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will try to be as brief as possible. This is a period of cooperation amongst the national parties. I think that in 1990, the end of 1990 and beginning of 1991, was marked by fair cooperation amongst the national parties, which resulted in the establishment of all republican organs in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The SDS policy was public. It was well known. There were major differences in the political concepts between the SDS, the HDZ, and the SDA, primarily in relation to the question of the survival, the political survival of Yugoslavia as a whole. This is about as much as I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, that's -- that's a helpful introduction so far as the three parties were concerned, then. And you said that the -- there were major differences. You said the SDS policy was public and it was well known. But I don't think you then went on to say, which I'm only inviting you to do in summary, Mr. Deronjic, to say what that policy was, as you understood it.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main political principle of the SDS of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was the preservation of a common state, the common state of Yugoslavia, in its federal form, and the position was to support the attempts by the Republic of Yugoslavia Presidency, the Presidency of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, to preserve Yugoslavia in its form, as it was at the time. This is the briefest way of putting it. I'm not going to talk about some secondary aspects of that programme.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Deronjic, you've done exactly what I was inviting you to do. May I offer you just a similar invitation, and inviting similar helpful brevity in relation to how you understood at the time that power-sharing structure was put together after the November 1990 elections, what you understood to be the essential policy of the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the war, I was able to meet with some leading figures from the SDA, and before the war also, and some local figures as well, with whom I worked each day. The SDA policy is something that I know, and in the political sense, they were in favour of, or the main position of their political programme was an independent, sovereign Bosnia and Herzegovina, which was a publicly proclaimed position. And I must say, then, that in that public part of it, it also described the new country as a democratic, sovereign Bosnia and Herzegovina. All of this was stated in their programme.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And similarly, again, just in very brief summary, what was your understanding, if any, at that time when the power-sharing structure was formed of the main policy of the HDZ, or HDZ perhaps?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my understanding, the division of power was based on partner relations. I didn't notice any dissatisfaction, except perhaps in some details. From what I was able to gather from the newspapers and the television, I didn't notice any dissatisfaction regarding this division. The policy of the HDZ was along the same political lines as the SDA's policy. They were also in favour of an independent, sovereign Bosnia and Herzegovina. And I think that as far as the general policy plans of the HDZ, it corresponded to those of the political party which was formed in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then do you remember that in February 1991, towards the end of February, Mr. Izetbegovic, who of course was SDA and was the president of Bosnia and Herzegovina, announced to parliament that he would sacrifice peace for a sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina, but for that peace in Bosnia-Herzegovina, he would not sacrifice sovereignty? Do you remember that particular occasion and statement?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that statement, absolutely. It was a major political statement, which was covered appropriately in all the media. I heard that statement, and it was something that was also commented at lower political levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, the -- it's correct, isn't it, that the Serb deputies in the Assembly refused to discuss a declaration of sovereignty. They took the view that that was unconstitutional.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember some details about that, which I heard indirectly over the media, and also through comments. The Serbian side considered that to be an unconstitutional attempt and that this was something that should be discussed by the council for interethnic relations, and only after that was the Assembly supposed to state its position on that. But I recall that it was considered to be an unconstitutional act. That's what I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you said that this was something that was also commented upon at lower political levels. That's what you said a moment ago. That's not a question, just a reminder, Mr. Deronjic. And you -- well, you very fairly acknowledged your own position in the political structure. You were -- is this fair: You were an important politician on the local level, you were at least a second-level politician once you got on to the national level?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I considered myself to be as the most important politician of the Bratunac municipality, and I believed also that I had influence at the regional level.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Deronjic, I'm not -- I'm not taking issue with you on that. You were clearly a very important person in Bratunac politics. That fed into the regional level. At the national level, of course, the policies were really in other hands largely, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with what you've just said. The answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But did you personally take the same view that you have summarised, that the proposals emanating from Mr. Izetbegovic and his party were unconstitutional?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I took the same view, except that I did not know the law or the constitutional articles so well. But I believed that this was not a proper act by the SDA, because it was being done against the will of the Serbian people. And I would just like to recall that the Serbian people were a constitutive part of the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So is this a fair summary, Mr. Deronjic, that again, as a -- well, an intelligent layman, but active in politics in your particular area, you had no reason to doubt your understanding of the party position on the unconstitutionality of what Mr. Izetbegovic and his party were proposing?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, we know now -- I don't think anybody seriously suggests this is an issue - you've mentioned it yourself - that in March 1991, there was a meeting between Mr. Milosevic, Mr. Slobodan Milosevic, and Mr. Tudjman, that's Mr. Franjo -- Franjo -- I think he's called Franjo Tudjman, in Karadjordjevo, in Northern Serbia. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that, and today I know that such a meeting was held. At the time, I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, it was at least when it first took place, it was apparently, wasn't it, a secret meeting?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can you remember when you personally first came to read or hear anything about that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember when I heard it for the first time, but I had -- I formed an opinion and I had information about that only after the war. Of course, this was talked about before, but I didn't have any proof or any confirmation for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But it's now well known, isn't it, Mr. Deronjic, that what Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Tudjman talked about and what they came to an understanding about was the division or, in English some would say a carve-up, of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is clear to me today, based on a series of documents and the testimony of people who spoke about it and who testified about it before this Tribunal also.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, you have talked in your evidence, Mr. Deronjic, about a meeting that took place in April 1991 in Sarajevo that you attended.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When Mr. Harmon was asking you questions, he said: "Do you know the meeting I'm talking about?" I'm going to ask exactly what Mr. Harmon asked. There's no better model. Do you know the meeting I'm talking about?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you -- you say it's a meeting of the Main Board. You can't remember the exact date, but I'm not going to trouble about that. You describe Mr. Karadzic having been there; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you said that -- the way you put it was: "Of course those meetings were also attended by the highest state officials, including," you said, "...members of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Mrs. Biljana Plavsic, Mr. Koljevic, although of course I can't say --" I'm quoting your evidence in this case: "Although of course I can't say with a hundred per cent certainty they were there, Mr. Krajisnik and so on, as far as I can remember, those were the attendees."
