So the position is you -- as I read your evidence there, Mr. Deronjic - please confirm - that naturally at that sort of meeting, the highest officials would have been there or represented. But in those particular cases, Mrs. Plavsic, Mr. Koljevic, Mr. Krajisnik, you can't say for certain which of them were there or if any one of them was -- was there; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's true that I cannot say that with 100 per cent certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you described this particular meeting as representing -- I think the phrase that came across was a new thrust in the policy of the SDS. And that is the way you viewed it, is it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the new thrust was this, wasn't it: That it was a recognition, if you like, wasn't it, of the possibility that federal Yugoslavia, including Bosnia and Herzegovina, might at some point cease to exist in its then-form?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And wasn't the position at that time that that was a recognition of the real world, that what had been happening, and, for example, what Mr. Izetbegovic was saying, and what had been happening generally, suggested that that was a possibility that could no longer be ignored?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This could not be ruled out. This, at the time, was quite a realistic fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So there was -- is this correct: In your view, there was nothing irresponsible about that suggestion being floated and discussed in some way at the meeting in April 1991?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was nothing which would indicate that it was not serious to discuss this topic at this meeting. I think that there was a natural need to discuss this topic at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, it could be put a little bit more -- I'm not disagreeing with that at all on Mr. Krajisnik's behalf, Mr. Deronjic. But it goes a little bit further, doesn't it, that Mr. Karadzic and anybody else supporting or associated with Mr. Karadzic would have been failing in their jobs if they hadn't recognised that possibility and considered it in some serious way?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that every politician should understand the point at which such a possibility was mentioned, and I already said that it was a realistic possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And in fact, your -- the precise words that you used earlier in your evidence in this case were that it was -- it was an idea that you yourself used later at some meetings at the local level.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I used them once or twice, I believe, at a public gathering, when I said that should a federal Yugoslavia disappear, then Serbs would ask for a partition of Bosnia. I believe I elaborated to this a bit further and said what it was that we would be requesting in that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, my colleague from the Defence quotes the testimony, or asserts to quote the testimony of Mr. Karadzic, but fails to discuss --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Deronjic, I think, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic. But fails to -- in his summaries of Mr. Deronjic's testimony, fails to include critical elements in it. I refer Your Honours to the page 72, in which the statements made by Mr. Karadzic weren't the recognition of the division but was the option to create a Greater Serbia. That's what the testimony of Mr. Deronjic was. It can be found on page 72, at lines 16 through 18. So if Mr. Stewart is going to quote, or purport to quote, the testimony of Mr. Deronjic, it is our position that he should quote it accurately and in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I don't have the slightest problem with that, Your Honour, because in the time that Mr. Harmon has been making his comments, I was moving on to that anyway. I don't have any intention of failing to grasp it, and no doubt if there's anything else that needs to be cleared up, re-examination will provide that opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, you -- I think you said a moment ago that you elaborated a bit further what it was that we would be requesting in the case of federal Yugoslavia disappearing. And I take it that when you say you elaborated a bit further, you mean in your discussions back in your own locality. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. With your permission, I can explain what I meant, if it's necessary for your purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, yes, please. Please do, Mr. Deronjic.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wanted to say that I spoke about the partition of Bosnia because after this meeting in Sarajevo, I had the opportunity of being with Karadzic in a small company, and he said that Bosnia would be divided or partitioned. So I used the same words. And not only that; I said that we would ask for a partition to take place. I didn't exactly say that an agreement had been reached to partition Bosnia, but that we would ask for the partition of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, in your evidence already given in this case, in describing what it was Mr. Karadzic said at the meeting, you said something which you then said was not a quotation but was the sense of what Mr. Karadzic said. And what you said before telling the Tribunal it wasn't a quotation but it was the sense of what he said, was that he said -- Mr. Karadzic said publicly that the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina and in Yugoslavia was such that if the federal Yugoslavia no longer existed, and it obviously didn't, then the only option open to the Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina is the creation of Greater Serbia. Do you remember giving that evidence?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, the first question -- you said this is not a quotation but is the sense of what he said. I just want to be clear whether you remember that, as part of what can be quoted, whether the phrase or the words "Greater Serbia" were included in what Mr. Karadzic said or whether that's a description of the sense.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The words "Greater Serbia" were used, and I can say with certainty that I probably quoted these words, perhaps not the whole sentence, but the words "Greater Serbia" definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, what did -- at the meeting, then, when you heard what Mr. Karadzic said, including that phrase, what was your understanding of what Mr. Karadzic was proposing, what he had in mind, so far as what he said, told you what was in his mind?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that point, I thought that this was a sentence which contains a kind of pressure and threat to the opposing political sides and that it was meant to be some sort of warning to the opposing sides. That is how I understood it at that moment. Because I was aware of the fact that politicians sometimes have the habit of exaggerating a little bit, so that they can elicit what they want to elicit from the other side. This is how I understood it and this is how I remember this. However, later, at a more private meeting that followed, I realised that this was a rather serious concept.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can I just pause, or just interrupt you for a moment, Mr. Deronjic. You have described the larger meeting and then the smaller, more private meeting already in your evidence. It's quite clear, isn't it, that as far as the smaller, private meeting is concerned, Mr. Krajisnik wasn't at that meeting, was he?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Right. And you were going on to say, then, that at the private meeting, you realised that this was a rather serious concept. Now, just what I want to ask you first is: What you understood the concept to be, what you -- you talked about a new thrust in SDS policy. What did you understand, overall, what Mr. Krajisnik was proposing -- I'm sorry, Mr. - slip of the tongue - what Mr. Karadzic was proposing, what did you understand that to entail?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The way I understood was that the survival of the common state of Yugoslavia, in particular, in its federal state, had been seriously brought into question. I had been following the events, and I myself was more or less of the same conviction. I was aware of what other participants in the discussion were saying and thinking. The attitude seemed to be non-reconcilable. It was a very serious political issue. And I understood that the will or the attitudes of the two other peoples of Bosnia and Herzegovina had already been clearly spelled out, that there should be an independent and sovereign Bosnia and Herzegovina, which was contrary to the positions expressed by the SDS, in terms of preservation of a common state of Yugoslavia. When the sovereignty and independence of Bosnia was about to be declared at the Assembly of the parliament, it was clear to me that the SDS policy was moving in a different direction, and I understood the President to mean that this was a new, a different political option for us, a new, a different political position as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, so far, Mr. Deronjic, you've described, if you like, the changed context, the changed situation, that the -- the possibility of breakup of Yugoslavia, with detachment of Bosnia and Herzegovina by way of becoming an independent, sovereign state, was -- had become a real possibility. That's where we -- that's where we got to, really, in the course of your evidence this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What I'm -- what I'm asking you about now, then, is that step one, if you like, is the recognition by the SDS and by Mr. Karadzic of that changed situation, that changed context, but then what did you understand to be the shift of policy of the SDS in response to that changed situation?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I have already answered, but let me repeat. My understanding was that from then on, the policy of the SDS was the partition of Bosnia and not the preservation of a unified Bosnia within a federal Yugoslavia. Of course, I have to say that my position was my own personal view, which I had formed. I did not take the floor at that meeting. I had simply formed this opinion. And once in Bratunac, I analysed the situation with my associates. We were trying to understand what this would imply. However, the events took place -- things happened very fast and I didn't have opportunity to verify what it really meant in terms of detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was any development of what it would actually mean or how it could be done - and I'm talking about partition now - the subject of discussion, first of all at the larger meeting of the two meetings that you've mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was no discussion about the details as to how it should be implemented. I said that in my view it was the first indication of the departure of the SDS from the initial policy, although at that moment we did not know exactly in which direction this was going to move, in particular when it comes to details.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And was there any such discussion of what partition might involve as a practical matter and how it might be done at the smaller of the two meetings that you've described?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You heard the phrase "Greater Serbia." Then did you have an understanding on that day of what that meant?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be frank, to this day I am not sure as to the exact meaning of the phrase "Greater Serbia." If it refers to the extension of the borders of the existing Republic of Serbia, then yes, I understood it to mean Greater Serbia, that is, something greater, larger, than that which existed at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And in your evidence earlier in this case, you described Mr. Karadzic as having said, at the smaller of the meetings, having made, you said, an additional comment to the effect that those who were afraid to take part in that - and he was talking about the division of Bosnia - should not take part in that. Afraid of what, did you understand Mr. Karadzic to be saying?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I will answer your question. But allow me to expand on this term "Greater Serbia," because I believe my answer was a little ambiguous a moment ago, so with your permission I should like to elaborate further.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said that to this date I was not aware of the exact meaning of "Greater Serbia," I was not referring to the political meaning of the term. I was referring to the word "greater." Historically speaking, Serbia had had different borders, depending on the epoch. At one point it extended as far as Greece. So I'm not sure as to which historical period they had in mind. Politically speaking, Greater Serbia is familiar to me from certain programmes, primarily of the Radical Party, when they spoke about the change of borders, Croatia, and the neighbours. But historically speaking, once again, I'm not sure as to what exactly they meant when they said "Greater Serbia," and I apologise for this digression. And let me now go back to your last question. My understanding was that any partition of Bosnia, be it an agreed one - and I was sure that it had not been agreed with either Muslims or Croats - maybe with Croats one could assume that such an agreement could be reached; however, it would be difficult to expect that. It was possible [as interpreted] to agree the partition of Bosnia with Muslims. So I thought that it would imply major political upheavals, including clashes and conflicts, so I thought that the position of Mr. Karadzic was a realistic attitude, a realistic view of the potential consequences of the policy that he had announced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, may I ask your attention for the transcript, especially page 53, line 6. I'm not quite sure whether there's not missing the word: "It was not possible to agree."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I think Your Honour is certainly right because after all it was only a couple of minutes ago and I distinctly remember that as Your Honour does. So I'm quite sure that the Court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please verify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The Tribunal's observation is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, I did understand that it was still -- you could assume that a partition of Bosnia could be agreed upon between, well, let's say, Serbs and Croats, but you would not think it to be possible to agree with the Muslims on the partition of Bosnia. Is that a correct understanding of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. This is my opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the word "not" is missing, and I have it in my ears, but I didn't see it with my eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It comes to exactly the same thing. Ms. Cmeric remembers that the word was "impossible" rather "possible," which is exactly the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Just following that up, then, Mr. Deronjic: You said that maybe with the Croats one could assume that such an agreement could be reached. Perhaps you could just explain very briefly why you made the assumption that it would be, well at least apparently easier to reach an agreement with the Croats?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will give you my personal opinion. I never tried to check that, but at various meetings we discussed this possibility as well, both at the -- including at the local municipal level. We believed that the interest of Croats with the respect of -- with regard to the partition of Bosnia could be identified with that of the Serbs, because they both have their mother states as well. And we thought that they could share the wish to join their territories in Bosnia and Herzegovina with their mother countries. As for the Muslims, it was obvious that they would not be prepared to accept such an option.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And so far as you were concerned, as a -- somebody coming from Bratunac to this -- these particular meetings, as far as you were concerned, was there anything irresponsible about the discussion and the ideas that were being floated at those meetings in April 1991?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't think that there was anything irresponsible in that. Apart from an opinion that I've formed later on, which can be found in the transcript of the meetings of the municipal board of the SDS, in late 1991 I made a protest because we didn't know what directions this policy would, practically speaking, take. We knew it was all about the partition of Bosnia, but we didn't know in practical terms in what way this policy would be implemented. You can find this in the transcripts of those meetings. Because I didn't want to participate in something that was not clear to me, that was a big unknown for me. But this was, as I indicated, in late 1991 or beginning of 1992, and you can find it in the minutes, in the transcripts of those meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, we considered in the course of your evidence this afternoon the run-up to April 1991. We've had those views of Mr. Izetbegovic expressed publicly, and we had, though not known at -- immediately at the time the meeting between Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Tudjman. It then -- do you recall it remained official SDS policy right through to the autumn of 1991 that Bosnia and Herzegovina should remain undivided and should remain part of Yugoslavia, the federal Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall such a view in specific terms that I read it or saw it somewhere. Maybe it did exist. If you could remind me of a particular statement, that might refresh my memory, but at this point, I really cannot recall any such statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm just asking you for your memory, Mr. Deronjic, so I won't go refreshing it on that issue. The --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. Just a small addition which might be of assistance to you. In the autumn of 1991, Bratunac saw a large number of conflicts. The town was visited by high-level delegations of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Those were very dramatic events, and this is the reason maybe why I missed a statement of that kind. Maybe I was not closely following the public pronunciations of such policies, including the policy of the SDS and other parties at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: There may have been some small misunderstanding with the language interpretation about what I was saying. That may not be so, but just in case: What you said in your evidence on, I think it was last Thursday, was that the SDS stood for the policy of preservation in Yugoslavia in the form it existed in, as a federal community of republics and officially that concept was valid until the fall or the autumn of 1991, when Republika Srpska was formed. That's what you said in your evidence. And that's what you remember as official policy?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. Officially, not a single SDS organ ever changed the basic political instrument, that is, the programme of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then you said in your evidence earlier in this case, you were asked by Mr. Harmon: "And following these particular meetings in April of 1991." You were asked whether you received instructions to prepare maps in respect of the ethnic composition of your municipality. And having been asked the question by Mr. Harmon in that form, you said: "Yes." Then you said: "In a certain period in 1991, we received orders from the party to prepare maps of our municipalities with as precise as possible representation of the ethnic structure in the territory of the municipality." Can you help on when you received such orders or instructions?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I cannot be precise. My approximation would be the summer of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So do you say it was definitely after those meetings in April 1991?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We drew the maps after that. I don't know. Maybe we created one such map at the very beginning of our political activities. I'm not sure. For instance, in my office at the SDS, I had a public map of Bosnia and Herzegovina which was marked with different colours and contained indications as to the composition of the population. So it was a public document at the time. I don't know whether at that period we also drew a map of that kind. I'm not sure. But definitely after the meetings, yes, we drew a number of maps, and I think we also added the information regarding the ownership of the land of Serbs in our municipality. You could find the percentages concerning the property, the ownership of land and forest, of the local population. I cannot remember precisely what else was there, but this would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you accepted and implemented those instructions in your own locality, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you saw nothing wrong with those instructions?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be perfectly frank, there were two streams, two currents. There was a lot of discussion about the formal ownership of Bosnia, in terms of landownership, and I remember discussions which involved our politicians, who spoke about the topic and who stated that, in terms of percentages, most of the land was in the hands of the Serbs. As for the drawing of those maps, I linked that event with the formation of the Association of Municipalities, which at one point came to be known as Serb autonomous regions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And those Serb autonomous regions, they started to be formed sometime in the summer of 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that that's the period of July and August 1991. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And there were five formed all together; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, except just four were formed in that period. The Autonomous Region of Birac, where I was, was formed in January or -- January of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Five all together, but Birac, which was yours, in fact, wasn't it? That's your region?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Six. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Six all together?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I'd like to ask for a clarification on an answer I have some difficulties in understanding. You told us about drawing maps, maps based on ethnicity of the population, but also on landownership. You said about two streams, and formal ownership of Bosnia in terms of landownership, and that it -- discussions were taking place in which politicians were involved. Was that on the local level or was that on the state level, that is, the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, the talks about the ownership of land in Bosnia and Herzegovina referred to talks conducted by top representatives of the political parties in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I've heard such arguments in numerous televised debates, discussions, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And was it an issue at a local level, or less?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Landownership is something that I don't recall discussing. I'm not saying that perhaps we didn't discuss it at the local level, but I'm not sure. It's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And talking about land ownership and that the majority of the land was owned by Serbs, is the meaning of the political argument that if there is not a majority in population, as far as number of inhabitants is concerned, that this could be compensated or that it would be also important, not only to know how many people of a certain ethnicity lived in the area but what part of that area was owned by persons of a specific ethnicity? Was that the meaning of this discussion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that was the meaning of this discussion. I just want to assist, but I'm afraid of making things more complicated. The SDA emphasised the demographic factor, the population figures, as an argument in debates about this perhaps weird question of who Bosnia and Herzegovina belongs to. The Serbs emphasised the historical arguments and land ownership. Croats had their own arguments, mostly historical arguments, about who was the ruler or who the rulers were at certain historical periods. So these were the main arguments of the opposing sides. I heard numerous arguments. Now it might seem a little strange that all these things were discussed, but they were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, just to make it clear, then: What -- you did prepare some maps, then, in your locality, did you, in response to the instructions you've mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And what was the nature of the maps that you prepared?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a map of the Bratunac municipality, with approximate markings in different colours of the ethnic composition of the municipality, in the territorial sense. The territorial distribution of Muslims, Serbs. It was quite a free estimate, because in mixed settlements, such as the Bratunac municipality and villages, it's difficult to say whether the territory belongs to one side or the other. Houses were all mixed together. There was no clear-cut division in this sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: How did -- just to be clear: How did you start, then? Did the -- was the -- well, I suppose the question I should ask first of all, Mr. Deronjic, is whether you were personally involved in the making up of any such map.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't make up any such map. This was done by a special service. It was usually the party secretary who dealt with this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You personally -- was there -- do you know: Was there one map or more than one map prepared in response to those instructions for your locality?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know and recall one. I'm not saying that there were no others, but I don't remember if that was so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And although you've given your answer about your own non-involvement in the preparation of that map, did you see that map when it had been prepared?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw it, certainly. I can't remember all the details, but I was familiar with it. This was something that we did openly in the office, and sometimes I was present while this was being done.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did it -- did the map take existing -- was it done this way: Did it take existing boundaries of units within the larger locality and then, in relation to each of those existing units, attempt to determine the ethnic composition?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot remember. I think that it was the -- a map of Bratunac. I don't know whether it was just done in freehand or if it was copied from somewhere in order to have the precise dimensions. I really cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can you remember the time scale for preparation of the map, from receiving the instructions to -- and you've already given evidence that it was sent to the Republican Party leadership. Can you remember how long that period was between the instructions and the sending off of the map to the leadership?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember without maybe making a mistake. I don't know why this is so relevant. I'm not avoiding it, but I really cannot remember what the time limit was. Perhaps it was done very quickly, but sent with a delay, or the other way around. I really cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you have any personal knowledge of whether, in 1991, any Muslim and/or Croat bodies or organisations or groups were engaged in any preparation of similar maps?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I do have personal knowledge. At the local level, I knew many members of the SDS municipal board from Bratunac. We would visit one another. We would go to each other's offices. They would look at our maps. I personally didn't see their maps, but I heard from their leaders that they were making similar maps depicting the ethnic composition of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I have some difficulties in understanding this answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps you have the same. Could you please clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You've referred -- it shows you say: "At the local level I knew --" it's come across in the transcript as: "Many members of the SDS municipal board from Bratunac." Do you mean SDS or do you mean -- well, do you mean SDS?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware -- there are two mistakes here. Maybe it's because of the interpretation or because I'm getting tired. It's not the Main Board of the SDS but the municipal board of the SDA. We were on friendly terms with some people from there. I knew them, of course. They were my neighbours, my colleagues. We lived in the same town. So they were members of the municipal board of the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I think that clarifies the point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It does. Mr. Stewart, we are close to 5.30. Would this be a suitable moment for a break?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I think so, Your Honour. The witness said he was feeling a bit tired, so perhaps that really would be a good point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll then adjourn until 10 minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I just wanted to mention where we were in relation to the question of the certification under Rule 73.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Which has rather been left open at the moment. The position now, Your Honour, is that taking what we think is a rather realistic view, we're not now going to continue to press for certification under that Rule, because, after all, the certification, is, as we read it, that is to allow us to proceed then with an interlocutory appeal as opposed to an appeal, and in the real world, it seems that this is not really the time to be pressing for that certification. So it remains, whatever that means, it remains an appeal point, but we no longer press for interlocutory appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You don't press for, that means that you withdraw the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The request for certification, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then please proceed with the cross-examination of Mr. Deronjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, the -- we were just talking about maps before the break. The maps were, you've already told the Court, in this case sent off to the republican leadership. You didn't personally send them, did you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember. Perhaps I did that personally, but usually this is done by the party secretary.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I forgot to put my headphones on, so I didn't ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it's an administrative -- it's an administrative secretarial matter simply to send them off to party headquarters, isn't it, or wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I said [Previous translation continues]... I said "them." I should say that, of course, it follows from the evidence, we don't actually know whether it's it or them, one map or more. I wasn't making -- or shouldn't have made any assumption there. The -- could we look at -- Your Honour, I'm not quite sure how this works mechanically for the witness. I want us to look, please, at P38.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It will be presented to the witness and then put on the ELMO, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm obliged, Your Honour. I take it that the witness and Mr. Krajisnik will obviously be looking at it in B/C/S, at the -- at that version, and the rest of us -- well, Ms. Cmeric can choose. The rest of us in the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you have that in front of you, Mr. Deronjic? That's the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The registrar is finding it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I have the document in front of me, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Deronjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So this is a document dated 15th of August, 1991, addressed to all municipal boards, which of course included Bratunac. We've looked at it before, but just to remind ourselves: The idea of it was -- the English translation is actually probably not the best that the translators have ever achieved, but the idea is that it's easy for members of the party to get out of touch with ordinary people who are not politically, actively involved. That's the particular point, isn't it, Mr. Deronjic? Is something going wrong with the mechanics? It seems the witness isn't hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you not receiving any translation, Mr. Deronjic? From your nodding, I do understand that you do not receive any translation. Madam Usher, would it be possible to find another earphone, headphone, so that we at least know whether it's caused by the headphone or by any other ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am getting a translation in these headphones, but I can also follow it to a certain extent in English. The translation does not contain the entire question put to me by Mr. Stewart. I don't believe it's an intentional mistake by the interpreters, but I believe that perhaps they didn't have time to interpret the entire question. So could you please repeat your question so that it could be translated completely to me. It refers to that part where you are talking about the separation of politics from the people, and she translated your question incorrectly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I first emphasise that mainly mistakes in translation are caused by the speed of speech. I would like to emphasise that. We earlier might have had a problem in transcribing as well. I will not hesitate to express my admiration for those who are transcribing and for those who are translating. If we slow down a bit, the risk of having any mistranslation, and it's of course human activity, subject to failure, as all our activities are, at least we minimise them. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Could I make a comment, Your Honour, because it occurs to me in all that slight confusion with the difficulties with the -- Mr. Deronjic's headphones, there may have been a misunderstanding. I did say, and I do say, that the translation of the particular document, P38, I said was not the best ever. In fact, frankly, it's a very poor translation. But that's got nothing whatever to do with the interpretation we're getting in Court today, which is another matter altogether.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I didn't understand it as any criticism on the interpreting services in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I was just afraid it might be taken that way with all the different points that were discussed. And I'll have in mind Your Honour's injunction not to go too fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, I'm going to start again on this question. I also -- please, I -- of course, I can't stop you, Mr. Deronjic, if you understand English and you understand my question, then I can't possibly obstruct you from that understanding, but it may be better if you leave deficiencies in the interpretation, as far as possible, to others to worry about, and concentrate simply on what you're getting through your headphones. But all I was going to say by way of introduction was that, do you agree, this is -- this document in the first place is directed towards a familiar problem, that those actively involved in politics can get out of touch with those people who are, understandably and admirably perhaps, just getting on with their lives and are not politically active?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Now I fully understand the question. When you have an opportunity to have a look at the transcript, you will see that the interpretation I received a moment ago was erroneous. Now it is quite clear that this document concerns the danger of bureaucratisation of the party, or rather, the party being estranged from the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So we're -- basically we're agreed, Mr. Deronjic, that the suggestion I put to you accords with your own view?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then it's -- there are specific -- there's a sort of system suggested then under the numbered points, and the particularly 4 and 5, that each member of a local board has a responsibility of keeping contact with 10 to 20 households and to report. Mr. Deronjic, is it fair to say that this was one of those very good ideas in theory, which was in fact extremely difficult to implement reliably in practice?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I think the question should be focussed on the municipality where this witness knows about this document and not so broad. I think it's too broad and too general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I understood the question to be about the personal experience of Mr. Deronjic in that municipality, but if I'm wrong, please reformulate the question. If I'm right, then perhaps the witness could answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour is right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then you may answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now we get -- we have a translation problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. So do we, Your Honour. A non-translation problem, actually, is what we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, could you please repeat your answer, because we did not get any translation.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I will repeat my answer. I said that I spoke about the issue of the implementation of all of the measures that had been given to us in forms of guidelines from the Main Board, and I said that it was impossible to implement some of those guidelines. Now, as to what is contained in item 4, this, for instance, was almost impossible to implement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We can put that on one side, then, thank you, P38. Now, just going back to the slightly broader picture, then,

utterances.speaker: MR. DERONJIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that in July 1991, which as it happens is just about a month before that particular document, but in July 1991, there was an agreement at the time regarded as historic, an agreement between Serbs and Muslims at a national level in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that Bosnia and Herzegovina would remain part of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall these events, though I cannot recall the exact date. But in Zvornik, for instance, I know that a meeting was held. If that is the meeting you have in mind, no, I did not personally attend it, although the venue was somewhere in the vicinity. But I was not informed of the meeting. The attempt to create a historical agreement between Serbs and Muslims in Bosnia and Herzegovina - that is how it was called - actually took place, and it resulted in a sort of agreement with a rather small party representing interests of Muslims in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the so-called MBO party. And it was with their leader that Karadzic [as interpreted] held a meeting in Zvornik. It was actually a public rally, and it constituted an attempt to reach this historical agreement. Of course, this small party was not representative of the overall interests of Muslims in Bosnia and Herzegovina, but obviously Karadzic [as interpreted] did not agree to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But it -- but it had the -- this agreement had -- either had or apparently had the support of Mr. Izetbegovic, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. So far as I can remember, he did not have that support. But I may be wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It could be actually that there has been an error, because you said: "This small party was not representative of the overall interest of Muslims in Bosnia and Herzegovina, but obviously Karadzic did not agree to that." It seems that you probably said Izetbegovic in that answer.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Izetbegovic. I'm almost certain that I said Izetbegovic. And I was referring to Izetbegovic, that he was the one who did not agree to the proposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think there seems to be some confusion. Where the name "Karadzic" appears, if that was the issue --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, that was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then it was -- the transcript says that: "And it was with their leader," I understood this to be the leader of the small Muslim party, that Karadzic held a meeting in Zvornik, and that Karadzic did not agree that the party, the small party, MBO, was not representative for the Muslim people. So I think, as a matter of fact, that it sounds quite logical to me -- I'm not expressing any other view on it. And later on, I do not think that the witness mentioned the name of Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, he did, Your Honour, at -- is it line -- page 70, line 2. I think that's what caused the confusion, because when the witness said Mr. Karadzic did not agree to that, I had assumed he was referring to the non-agreement earlier about the non-representative nature of the party. In fact, it seems that that was simply an error and that he did actually refer to Mr. Izetbegovic in that second answer. And it got -- it came across in the transcript then as Karadzic, instead of Izetbegovic. I hope that's crystal clear, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have no problems in understanding, and I do understand that Mr. Karadzic did not agree with the fact that it was not representative, so that he considered this small party to be representative for the Muslim population. That's how I understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. And then the witness was going on to make it clear and he's clarified that then that his evidence is that Mr. Izetbegovic did not agree with the agreement at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you will allow me, Your Honours, I would like to explain this particular sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If Mr. Stewart needs any further explanation he'll ask you for it. If not, I have no difficulties at this moment to understand what your testimony until now was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I think, Your Honour, I would -- we've been having this debate over the last couple of minutes but it is Mr. Deronjic who is the witness. I believe I would prefer him to have the opportunity of explaining.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Please do, Mr. Deronjic.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a slip. I said Karadzic did not agree with that. So it must have been a slip of the tongue. Karadzic endeavoured to obtain an agreement, and this agreement was interpreted in Bosnia and Herzegovina as a historical agreement. I wanted to say that this was not representative of the will of the Muslim people because of the very small size of this particular party, and the view of Mr. Izetbegovic of this agreement was, in my opinion, negative. And if you will allow me one more sentence. I've been having this feeling that you want me to be totally consistent when it comes to details. It's very hard for me. This pressure will only make me -- make more mistakes. It's very difficult to -- for me to be mindful of every single word. I have so far provided testimony and given statements containing hundreds of pages, and it is very easy to make mistakes and slips of this kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Deronjic, I'm sure that His Honour would support me in this: The translation or interpretation element makes life more difficult for everybody, so it's perfectly natural that slips get made from time to time. Everybody understands that. That isn't a problem at all. We have to sort it out from time to time when it happens. That's number one. Number two is: I only want you to give the Tribunal detail when you are able to and when you actually do truthfully and genuinely remember. Because what the Tribunal wants, I feel confident, and what we want, is that when you can't remember detail, you say you can't remember detail. When you do remember detail reliably, you say so. That, I believe, is all that is required.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I hope, Your Honour, that's a fair summary of what we're all looking for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Deronjic, don't get nervous. Everyone is aware that there are a lot of details, and just try to concentrate and answer to the best of your ability the questions, and there will be no problem. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then moving forward, then, to 14th, 15th October, 1991, even if you don't remember the exact date, Mr. Deronjic, but do you remember at that time that there was a very significant event, which was that in the Bosnia and Herzegovina Assembly, the Muslim and Croat deputies voted for a declaration of independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina after the Serb deputies had walked out of the session?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I clearly remember this event. I remember when the session was held. I remember watching it on TV in direct, together with my father.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. And I think the reason I say 14, 15th October I think is because -- not because anybody doesn't know the date, but it started on the 14th and it went on very late at night into the 15th. That's what happened, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were you watching it on television?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And in fact, Mr. -- now, Mr. Krajisnik was involved, naturally, wasn't he, because he was the Speaker, Mr. Krajisnik, remained for a very short time simply to close the -- formally, as far as he was concerned, formally close the session?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. After the walkout, Mr. Krajisnik stayed there for a while, trying to conclude formally the session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But then he left, but the Muslim and Croat deputies continued the session?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Continued in at least the practical sense, that they carried on debating and passing a resolution?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And that was -- that proceeding was that -- after Mr. Krajisnik had closed the session and left, that was regarded by the Serb deputies and the -- in fact, the wider Serb community as unconstitutional, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We believed it to be unconstitutional.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Or invalid in the sense that it wasn't a proper session of the Assembly once Mr. Krajisnik had purported to close it and had left. That was the view, wasn't it, the Serb view?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct, if we are talking about the entire Serb population. I'm not sure that everybody is aware of the legal regulations. But we believed at least that it was an unjust decision, because it had been adopted in the absence of the Serb deputies in the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Deronjic, I wasn't going so far as to suggest that every single Serb -- you're quite right, that every single Serb in the country had a view about the constitutionality. It's after all possible to find people around here who don't have a decided view on the social charter of the European Union. Mr. Deronjic, could we move forward, please, to December 1991. Mr. Harmon asked you about a meeting on the 19th of December, 1991, but I think it has been clear throughout previous evidence that you have given and in your view that you're not absolutely sure of the date of the meeting, and I think you know the meeting we're talking about, where you've given evidence about variants A and B. You're not a hundred per cent sure of the date, are you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not sure about the date of this meeting. But what assisted me to a certain extent was the fact that after the interview, I was able to see the minutes of the municipal boards once again. So I think that I am now in a better position to say that the meeting took place on the 19th, because the consequence was a meeting held in Bratunac right after that. I was not sure whether it was before the session, and I know that the session was held either on the 20th or the 21st, or after the session. But I remember seeing all of the participants of the session attending this meeting. So I am sorry if I was not able to be precise, but I was not sure if it was before or after the session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, that's the evidence you've already given in this case. And in your earlier evidence, on Friday - I think that must have been - yes, Friday the 13th, you made two points. First of all, you said that at that meeting you saw, as far as you could remember, the top officials of the SDS, including the party Presidency, including Mr. Krajisnik, who was preparing the Assembly session. Your reference to preparing the Assembly session rather implies that the meeting must have taken place before the Assembly session. Does that sound right to you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it sounds quite probable.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then you say, of course, all the members of the Main Board were present. But then you also said in your evidence, to make it brief -- I'm not trying to catch you out here, Mr. Deronjic. I'm just trying to get things clear. You said: "To make it brief, it was a well-known event attended by all the top party officials and people who to date had participated in a joint authority, Mr. Koljevic, Mrs. Plavsic." You say: "I'm not sure whether I saw all of them. But I did see some of them." So although you were suggesting that in general terms all the top leadership were present, it seemed that in any individual case, you weren't a hundred per cent sure. Is it the position that you can't be sure in the case of Mr. Koljevic, Mrs. Plavsic, or Mr. Krajisnik in any specific case, you can't be a hundred per cent sure whether they were there or not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose I could agree with your position. Yes, that was -- that is the answer, with a caveat, however. As regards Mr. Krajisnik, I indicated that I was not sure that he had attended this meeting when the Variant A and B was discussed, but I am sure that I saw him there on those days, because at that time there was also a session that was held there. So my memory is linking the session, which I know took place at that time, and seeing him. I think, I believe, I saw him on that occasion, and I apologise if there is any contradiction in what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, just -- you've just appeared to be clarifying what you've said. So if Mr. Krajisnik -- if Mr. Krajisnik's position is, which in fact it is, that he wasn't at the meeting where you described Variants A and B and having been handed out, then your position is you wouldn't dispute that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the position of Mr. Krajisnik, but I have no reason to doubt that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, Mr. Deronjic. No. I was trying to help by telling you what Mr. Krajisnik's position is. Mr. Krajisnik's position is that he was not at that meeting. So I'm saying that being his position, you would be willing to accept that, would you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For reasons of my being unable to claim that he was present with certainty, yes, I will accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Could you describe exactly when in the course of that meeting, and whether at the beginning, during the meeting, at the end, as people were leaving, but whenever in that timescale these documents, or this document containing Variant A and B, was received by you.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. I have to give you a brief introduction. When I thought about this issue, about this question, because I had already received it from the Prosecutor, I was unable to remember this particular session. I said that it was a matter of practice for us to receive these documents, including guidelines and instructions, after the session, in an envelope mostly, except in cases where the documents were work documents which needed to be discussed at the meeting or at the session. So it is possible that we received this particular document before, but maybe it was after. I don't know. I cannot tell you exactly when it was that I personally received the document during that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And just to clarify: The document -- well, perhaps you can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's P43, Your Honour. I'm not sure it will matter, but apparently the interpretation came across as P44. But I suppose the witness will get P43 anyway, so it won't matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stewart, if during a break you would have an idea on what documents you want to show to the witness in cross-examination, could you perhaps give a brief note to the registrar so that she can prepare already for the documents to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that, Your Honour. We shall do that. In fact, I think this is going to be the last one this afternoon. But I take the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We've still got quite a ways to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I have taken the point, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: First of all, it's -- the -- this number 100, that is actually -- that's actually the one that you received, is it? Do you see, top right-hand corner on the first page, where the number 100 is written? That's actually the one that you received, is it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say with precision whether this is the document that I received, whether this particular document is the one. I never gave it to anyone. I really cannot say that this is the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The -- what exactly do you say you were told about this document, then, orally in the course of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing I can say with certainty and precision is that I remember Karadzic's explanations concerning some of the positions explained in these variants, in the first and the second stage of their implementation. I remember - and this is what I remember best - was -- I remember the explanation as to how the people on the ground should be kept in contact with local boards, and also with municipal boards [as interpreted]. This is something that I remember. And yes, more or less I do remember the discussion of these items, but I couldn't add anything specific to these -- to the explanation given.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When you -- you talk about the discussion of keeping in touch, people on the ground should be in contact with local boards and with municipal boards, when you say: "People on the ground should keep in touch with local boards and municipal boards," I'm trying not to be nit-picking about it, Mr. Deronjic. It's the other way round. It's the local boards and the municipal boards keeping in touch with the people on the ground, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And when you gave evidence on Friday about this meeting, you said you were only -- you said very frankly, you were only able to quote one sentence spoken by Mr. Karadzic, that you, the local representatives there, were duty-bound to ensure contacts with every man - they were thinking of Serbs in the municipality, and if possible, to ensure physical contacts. And then it was suggested the municipal boards should distribute amongst the officials in the local boards the number of families that they would be in charge of. Now, that sounds, Mr. Deronjic, very like the document that we looked at a few minutes ago, P38 was the reference, the August 15th document, that you had said was so very difficult, practically impossible, to implement in practice. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It sounds like the item from the earlier instructions on the conduct of the party. But I would like to say that these explanations and Mr. Karadzic's speeches are something that I recall from this meeting, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, I'm not -- I'm not in a position to challenge your recollection of that at this meeting. The suggestion I was putting to you was that that particular bit of what Mr. Karadzic was saying to you sounds like an exhortation and a reinforcement of what was in the August 15th document.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you know yourself who prepared the document that you're now looking at, P43, the instructions, the Variant A and B instructions for organisation and so on?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally don't know, except that I could have read that this was material of the Main Board. And I can say that I focussed my attention in more detail on this when I found myself here in the courtroom, or in detention, and when I saw that document, for a time, I even thought that perhaps this was even an Assembly conclusion, which turned out to be quite an incorrect view.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm just trying to get clear, Mr. Deronjic, that -- is the position that -- you can read on this document, of course, left-hand top corner of the cover sheet, "Serbian Democratic Party, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Main Committee." You see that, don't you, in the top left-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And with respect, we can all read that in either B/C/S or English. The question --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The upper left-hand corner in the P43 should read: "Main Board," not "Main Committee."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's absolutely right. I've got -- the one I had got said, "Main Committee," and the one I've just been handed says, "Main Board." I accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The one in evidence says, "Main Board."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The one in evidence says, "Main Board." For some reason, I had another one. My apologies. With a bit of luck, it will have got translated into B/C/S exactly the same way anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But to avoid any possible confusion: Top left-hand corner, cover sheet, it says: "Serbian Democratic Party of Bosnia and Herzegovina," and then in English translation: "Main Board." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it in the English version, and also in the translation it says: "Main Board."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Mr. Deronjic, you can manage the English version as well without difficulty. But is this the position: That you actually yourself from your personal knowledge, you don't know more than anybody else here beyond those words printed on the page as to who actually prepared this document originally?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know anything about it directly, except that we implemented the various stages of this document in Bratunac, in consultation with the party Presidency and in consultation with Mr. Zekic, who was a member of the Main Board and who informed us about the various stages of the implementation of this document. And I thought that this was quite sufficient. I personally received it at the Main Board, so I had no doubt that this was an authentic document of the SDS Main Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you in fact know if it was ever formally approved or adopted by the SDS Main Board?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know and I didn't check it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Is it correct: It wasn't actually presented at that meeting as official SDS -- an official SDS policy document, was it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand completely the sense of the question. Which meeting are you thinking of, and what is the gist of the question? Could you please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. The meeting I'm talking about -- yes, I understand. We moved on to the locality. The meeting I'm talking about is the one in Sarajevo on the 19th, as you seem to feel it probably was now, at which Mr. Karadzic spoke. So that's the meeting I'm talking about. And the -- what I was putting to you was that at that meeting, this document was not in fact presented as official SDS policy.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember it being adopted, so, according to my recollection, it was not. I don't remember anyone saying that this is a document adopted by the Main Board. This is something that I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, did you, having, as you've given evidence, then, taken this document away from the meeting on the 19th of December, did you -- not necessarily that night or that day, but did you immediately, or soon after that meeting, personally study it in detail?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did study it, and I implemented it at a meeting in Bratunac, or, actually, interpreted it at the SDS board meeting in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And of course it was Variant B which was applicable to Bratunac, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were there -- and I'll put the question this way: Did you have any doubts or misgivings about the Variant B content of this document either as a matter of principle, whether it ought to be aiming to achieve and instruct what it was aiming at and instructing, or, secondly, as a matter of practice, in terms of whether what it aimed to achieve could actually be done? Just -- before we go any further into that: Did you have misgivings in either of those areas, one and two?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, may I invite you to instruct the usher exactly to at what page. Because we're now not talking about the cover page any more, but about Variants A and B, what page to be put on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. It's page 5 in both English and in B/C/S, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could page 5 be put on the ELMO. And, Mr. Stewart, I just remind you, that whatever discussions you have with the team, if you leave the microphone open, we will be able to follow. If that's your intention, fine. If you'd rather not everything to be overheard, please switch off your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's a helpful and timely reminder. I don't think any great disaster occurred with that particular exchange, Your Honour, but thank you for the warning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's why I say it now and not --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Deronjic. You see Variant B beginning at page 5. And I'll put the question again. It was rather a long question, so I'll break it into -- it turned out much longer than I had hoped. I'll break it into two. First of all, did you yourself have any misgivings about the Variant B proposals here, in principle, in the sense of whether these were proper aims for the party to be, as you understood it, to be instructing?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is two parts to the answer. The one referring to the Variant B is as follows: I said at the municipal board that the first stage of Variant B was something that I didn't have any principle dilemmas about, and I said that we were duty-bound to implement that as part of the state policy and instructions issued to us by the top leadership of our party. And this is stated in the minutes from that meeting. However, when Goran Zekic informed the Bratunac municipal board and myself personally that the second stage of Variant B was being introduced, doubts appeared whether this was possible, and I also had some personal dilemmas about the propriety of this policy. There are minutes from those meetings, in which it can be seen that I even submitted my resignation, not wishing to embark on the implementation of these objectives. I felt that this would lead to war, and this is what I said, and that sentence of mine is written down in the minutes of that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So this is the second stage that provoked those concerns on your part; that's right, is it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You didn't have -- you didn't personally have any problem, as a matter of principle, with the first stage?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: If we look at -- well, it's the foot of page 5 in the English version. It may be around the foot of page 5 or the top of page 6 in the B/C/S version. There's a sentence that says: "The commander shall appoint a member of the Crisis Staff to coordinate relations with the municipal leaderships of the SDA and HDZ." Do you see that? Well, you can cross-check the English, I think, Mr. Deronjic, as well.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot find it. Could you please help me, tell me which paragraph it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's the very end of item 3. First stage, number 3. Well, it's immediately before you get to point numbered 4. It's a couple of lines. So Variant B first stage, very last bit of item 3.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've found it and I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: "The commander shall appoint," and so on. So you've read it. And that happened, did it, in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I coordinated those relations with the SDA and the HDZ. Well, actually, there was no HDZ in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I beg your pardon. So -- and you were, in the terminology here in English, you were the commander, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Commander of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Well, you were the person, it's translated into English here as the commander. Yes. So in effect -- well, it seems we're not really -- don't really have an issue here. It says the commander shall appoint a member of the Crisis Staff. In effect, you appointed yourself. That's not a criticism, Mr. Deronjic; it's just a suggestion. That's in effect what happened; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even if we had appointed somebody - I really don't remember whether we did or not - I was the one who maintained contacts with the SDA board.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: All right. And then when we -- so when we get to the second stage, then, and that's over on page 7 of the English version, it begins, I think, at the very foot of page 7 of the B/C/S version as well. What were the -- it's divided up into seven points, and then we've got four points at the end, which are I think general, in fact, as far as this document is concerned. Can you tell Their Honours which of those points under second stage were the ones that did cause you the personal dilemma, I think was the way you put it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Second stage of the organising of the Serbian people and its institutions implied the creation of parallel organs entirely. The first stage provided for the preparation for the possible establishment of those organs, and second stage meant the actual establishment of such organs. And the complete withdrawal from joint bodies of authority, which we shared with the SDA. That stage called for a unilateral break in relations, and practically meant the destruction of the municipal institutions by the Serbs. Because we did participate in the governance to date and we had key functions. The president of the Executive Board was a Serb. If we withdrew him and the Executive Board member and the Main Board member, we then practically destroyed or dismantled that institution. I was not ready for such a radical act, and this prompted certain dilemmas on my part. If I am absolutely precise, my main objection was over the fact that we did not sufficiently explain. We were ordered or instructed to do something, but the specificity of certain regions was a key, and the most important factor there. If I carried this out in Bratunac, I could cause the outbreak of war, and I did not want to be the cause for war breaking out in the municipality of Bratunac. So this was the reason for my dissatisfaction, the fact that nobody fully considered the effect of such steps, what the consequences would be of the implementation of such actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Are you saying that -- well, in your own locality, for example, in Bratunac, was your view within the active SDS organs, was your view a minority view?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My view at the board was a minority one in the beginning, and that is why I submitted my resignation. As the meeting continued, we discussed this within the municipal board Presidency, and I received certain promises, to the effect that I could adapt those orders to local conditions in the Bratunac municipality. So that was the condition under which I withdrew my resignation, and then we discussed at the municipal board how we would implement this in Bratunac. What I am trying to say is that I felt responsible for the implementation of decisions of my organs, but on the other hand I felt fear because of that. So due to my inability to resolve that, I submitted my resignation. But when I received assurances that locally we could do this in a calmer way, I withdrew my resignation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So is this the position, then, Mr. Deronjic: You were initially in a minority view, in the sense that you were far gloomier and more pessimistic about the consequences of implementing these measures than your -- the majority of your colleagues?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I was outvoted on that position. The majority of the municipal board members believed that we should implement these points consistently.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And they were less -- they were less pessimistic than you, then, as to where this might lead and your view that it would lead on to war?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you could put it that way. Despite a little explanation here. Despite the fact that the party had enough time to make proper boards to assemble intellectuals from those communities, unfortunately, we did not manage to put together in the intellectual sense proper committees. In my board there were five or six of us who, conditionally speaking, were intellectuals. The rest of the members who people who, I would say, did not even have a developed political position and were not up to coordinating their positions along the lines of the current political situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
